title: Efficient Data Movement with Copy Atoms in CuTe DSL
key_concepts: Copy atoms for efficient data transfer
Async copy and TMA for latency hiding
critical_patterns: GMEM to RMEM: Use vectorized loads for efficient register usage
GMEM to SMEM: Employ async copy for non-blocking transfers
SMEM to RMEM: Optimize for MMA preparation
RMEM to GMEM: Use vectorized stores when aligned
constraints: Synchronize threads after shared memory writes
Avoid size and type mismatches in copy operations
Use async copy and wait for completion before accessing data
compressed_summary: Copy atoms in CuTe DSL are essential for efficient data movement across different memory spaces, leveraging hardware-optimized instructions like vectorized loads, async copy, and TMA. They encapsulate source and destination memory spaces, data layout, and hardware instructions, acting as templates for data transfer. Basic operations can be performed using direct assignment for simple element-wise copies, but copy atoms are preferred for moving data tiles, requiring vectorization or async operations. For GMEM to RMEM transfers, vectorized loads are recommended, while GMEM to SMEM transfers benefit from async copy on Ampere architectures or TMA on Hopper. SMEM to RMEM transfers should be optimized for MMA preparation, and RMEM to GMEM transfers should use vectorized stores when aligned. Key performance optimizations include coalescing global memory accesses, avoiding shared memory bank conflicts through padding, and maximizing bandwidth by vectorizing aligned accesses. Common errors include size and type mismatches, and missing synchronization after shared memory writes. Debugging can be facilitated using print statements before and after copy operations. Best practices involve using copy atoms for tile transfers, synchronizing after shared memory writes, and leveraging architecture-specific features like Ampere's cp.async and Hopper's TMA for enhanced performance.
